records.title: β-Ocimene in plant ecological interactions
records.statement: β-Ocimene is widely emitted from flowers and leaves and has been associated with floral visitor interactions and herbivory-induced plant defense signaling across many plant species.
records.organismContext: Multiple plant families, floral visitors, herbivores, and higher-trophic-level organisms reviewed across published studies
records.evidenceBasis: Review of published floral and foliar volatile ecology studies
records.notes: The review discusses β-ocimene broadly and does not establish that every reported ecological role is attributable separately to the E or Z isomer.

records.title: (E)-β-Caryophyllene as an herbivore-induced belowground defense signal
records.statement: Maize roots damaged by western corn rootworm larvae released (E)-β-caryophyllene, which attracted entomopathogenic nematodes; field manipulation of the signal altered nematode infection and adult beetle emergence under the reported conditions.
records.organismContext: Maize roots, Diabrotica virgifera virgifera larvae, and entomopathogenic nematodes in laboratory and field experiments
records.evidenceBasis: Compound identification, behavioral/attraction experiments, field comparisons, and authentic-compound soil manipulation
records.notes: Ecological plant-defense evidence in maize. It does not imply the same ecological function or emission pattern in Cannabis.

records.title: Linalool across floral attraction and plant-defense interactions
records.statement: A plant-ecology review describes linalool and its enantiomers/metabolites as participating in a broad range of plant-pollinator and plant-defense interactions, with behavioral responses depending on enantiomer, mixture, ratio, species and ecological context.
records.organismContext: Multiple plant species and floral visitors/herbivores reviewed across published ecological studies
records.evidenceBasis: Review of floral volatile ecology, sensory discrimination, pollinator behavior, and plant-defense studies
records.notes: The chapter identity is non-enantiomer-specific linalool. Individual ecological outcomes may be enantiomer-specific and should not be generalized across all linalool forms.
